title: Continuous Mistake
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart
summary: The talk's main teaching is that imperfection and mistakes are an inherent part of life, and it's through embracing these flaws that we can develop greater awareness, self-love, and acceptance. By letting go of our attachment to certain narratives and expectations, we can cultivate a more open and loving mind, allowing us to connect with something greater than ourselves and find freedom in the present moment. This process is not about achieving perfection, but rather about embracing the beauty and complexity of life as it unfolds.

sentences.text: Good morning, friends.
How are you?
I'm really happy to see so many of you here after yesterday.
Some of you had the opportunity to come to our practice period opening retreat.
If you didn't, there's still the closing retreat in March.
The retreat yesterday was really wonderful and warm-spirited.
It was so good to sit with about 30 people, even though I could only see them on the screen of my little laptop.
I still see Desiree in my main picture, so somehow it doesn't believe that I'm the speaker.
But that's alright, too.
It was just really wonderful yesterday, even though it was only laptop community.
I had this great feeling of contentment and peace, just this.
Today's opening poem is by my beloved teacher, Norman Fischer.
I have read it before, and I'll probably read it again at some time in the future, because I really love it.
It's rather complex, so I'm intentionally reading it twice.
The title is "Responsibility," and I hope that you love this poem as much as I do.
*Responsibility.
Tonight, it's quiet.
Or in the quiet.
Or, at least, the quiet is all around us.
What is it I'm worried about when I worry about anything?
What is it I tangle up in wanting to go home?
From down here, I look up at myself in the little bright square of window, staring down at me in bemusement, querying.
What's it worth?
But that's a question snaps shut on itself.
Thoughts with teeth and claws to scrape away to the very core.
What cares contains its value.
Half-life?
Mixed?
No doubt?
Yet fair.
It's always fair.
Or anyway, it's always what's there, and it's not our fault.*

Or in the quiet.
Or, at least, the quiet is all around us.
What is it I'm worried about when I worry about anything?
What is it I tangle up in wanting to go home?
From down here, I look up at myself in the little bright square of window, staring down at me in bemusement, querying.
What's it worth?
But that's a question snaps shut on itself.
Thoughts with teeth or claws to scrape away to the very core.
What cares contains its value.
Half-life?
Mixed?
No doubt?
Yet fair.
It's fair.
Or anyway, it's always what's there, and it's not our fault.*
Norman once did a dharma talk about this poem, and I really loved what he said in the end, after "it's not our fault."
He said, "And yet, it is our responsibility."
It is not our fault.
It is our responsibility.
What a difference.
I hope that maybe you get to love this poem as much as I have loved it for years.
It's in the poetry collection *Slowly But Dearly*.
A little warning: the next bit of the dharma talk is self-referential.
Mostly that's because I can only talk about my own mental states, not anybody else's, so I use myself.
Also, I make a really good bad example.
I will let you in on a bit of a secret.
Probably it's not a secret for Desiree, who is our steady doanryo for Zen life, and many would not have picked up on it yesterday.
So here it is: I sometimes have bouts of insomnia that are really gnarly.
According to my Fitbit, during Friday night I got two hours and 27 minutes of sleep.
So when the retreat rolled around yesterday at 7am, I was in a daze.
In expert language, I was what you'd call wonky.
I was totally out of it.
Somehow during the Han roll down, opening the retreat, for which I use my phone as a timer and for the Han pattern both, I turned off my phone.
I still don't know how.
Also, last week, just before Zen Alive, sometime between 9:30 and 9:40, my laptop broke.
So I'm using this ancient loaner laptop right now, and my Zoom settings were not right.
Several people were kind enough to inform me of that in the chat feature: turn on this, change that setting, do this, do that.
I did all that, but somehow I must not have saved it, so I got a bunch more messages.
By that time I was so frazzled that I forgot to turn off the mute button, so people heard every mouse click and key click while I was trying to fix myself and my laptop.
Between all that, I also got lost in the Han pattern, and the laptop wasn't transmitting the ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta-ta.
Tim figured out that I must have been done with the Han pattern and just started with the rope chant, and thereby saved my butt.
So all this is going on in my mind and practice there.
It doesn't really harm anybody, though people might have thought that I'm a total goofball and losing it.
Let me say this: that whole thing with making mistakes totally continued throughout the whole day yesterday.
The good thing is probably not too many people picked up on it.
I did the best I could.
I realized that in a way this is a very accurate description of moving through life: one continuous mistake.
When I started to practice Zen more intensely, more than 20 years ago, I wondered how come I had not noticed that before.
In fact, I thought that Zen practice was causing me to make more mistakes, which actually wasn't true.
I just noticed it more.
I investigated it a bit, and I realized that in what we call normal life, one activity, one event chases the next.
I don't just sit down and become more aware of what is going on.
No, I sit down, I read a book.
I don't just get up.
I get up to get something to drink or to answer the phone or whatever.
I might get up to go work on a project.
I don't notice the getting up and the going.
I certainly try to do things mindfully, but doing, in our brain the way we are wired, seems to override the being.
The other aspect is the precision of Zen forms.
They let me know precisely when I mess up.
They also let me know when everything is running smoothly.
It is not only the intellectual "I got this," but a feeling deep in my body when the forms flow without oopses, when things happen without resistance.
Slowing down, being aware and mindful of what I do, having no agenda beyond the current activity, life reveals itself.
And I'm not getting up to go do a project.
I'm getting up to get up.
When I sit, I sit to sit.
When I stand, I stand to stand.
Thank you for listening to some of the things that were going on in my mind yesterday.
But something else was going on too: twenty years of practice showed up.
Twenty years of practice said, "Yeah, I didn't do exactly what the script said I should do right now," and didn't get stuck on it.
Not getting fried, not chasing the mistakes of the past, but making new ones and being present for those too.
It was a really wonderful retreat.
Do I wish I had been a picture-perfect Eno?
Probably yes, but I have no energy on it.
I am not thinking, "Oh, I'm such a loser, a failure, a bad person, because I made four mistakes yesterday."
I didn't follow the script closely.
I did apologize to Tim.
I said to him, "Hey, from here on out, it can only get better or worse."
It'll change.
We both had a good laugh.
So no doubt it will change.
It will be different.
Another important thought is that exactly this is practice.
This is serving Buddha, Dharma and Sangha, and in serving Buddha, Dharma and Sangha, we save ourselves.
I save myself.
I connect with something that is definitely greater than myself, and while I do this, I get to spend time with cherished friends.
This love is like a layer on top of everything that is going on.

The conditioning I received in my childhood, both from school and my parents, wants me to believe that this Chris who made all these mistakes is an unlovable loser, unworthy, and I should think twice about raising my hand to volunteer for anything in the future because, you know, I just can't hack it.
Nah.
Conditioning is something really interesting too.
I'm getting better at figuring out how this conditioned mind is working.
I don't believe any longer that this conditioning, this judging mental overlay, is who I am.
I call my conditioning the judge.
It's definitely male, and it talks to me in unkind terms.
It used to be really harsh.
Then I invented this little creative trick for when the judge shows up and starts telling me who I should be or what I should be or what I did wrong again.
I say, "Hey, do you want to sit down for a cup of tea?"
We sit down on the park bench, and he tells me all about it, and I listen to it patiently.
I don't argue with the judge.
I do get pretty good at ignoring him at times.
The judge tells me who and what I am, what is possible for me and what is not possible for me.
Like I said, I'm not buying this storyline anymore.
I have moved from believing I am what my conditioning says to observing the judge, observing my conditioning.
And yes, that judge keeps on showing up.
I think he climbs in through windows, or he has an extra key for my front door.
He comes in the back door.
He uses my blind spots and sneaks up on me.
Conditioned mind also redirects our focus from process to content.
It gets stuck with little details and not with how all this happens.
The judge wants me to be stuck in the problem position, because that's how conditioning retains power.
So, dear friends, let's not be chained, and let's not chain ourselves to damned if you do and damned if you don't.
It's not an either-or thing.
Conditioning thrives when we cling to one aspect and reject its opposite.
By being present with reality, we can change the relationship with the conditioned mind, with our habit energy, and with the freedom that comes with it.
The freedom that comes with acceptance is delicious.
The world is not our fault, and yet it is our responsibility.
*From down here, I look up at myself in that little bright square of windows staring down at me in bemusement, querying, what's it worth?
But that's a question snaps shut on itself, thoughts with teeth and claws to scrape away to the very core.
What cares contains its value, its half-life.*
And you may see, if you see me on your screen, that the sun is really out, and isn't that wonderful?
After so many days of gray and dark, it's blinding.
We'd like to circle back and talk a little bit about practice periods.
I applaud Hannah, our Shuso this year.
It takes courage to give a seeking mind talk in this setting, before the Sangha and one's teachers.

I don't know about Hannah, but there's this feeling of being utterly exposed, bared, no way to hide and not wanting to hide, not wanting to show the world this perfectly made-up face, no wrinkles, young forever, perfect, nothing bad ever happened, I'm perfect.
To stand for one's continuous mistakes and love and glory, to stand for what happened.
I don't mean to imply blame, quite the opposite.
Facing what is there, not turning away from what is hard and painful, without complaint.
I applaud anyone and everyone who passes through this Dharma gate, because that's what it is.
No doors, no door frame, invisible, and it's huge.
The thought that so many Zen centers in the US, in Europe, in Asia, in Africa have annual practice periods with Shusos, living the self-inquiry, moves me deeply, and it gives me hope for us humans.
And yes, it has nothing to do in a way with being Shuso, because we are [unclear: "lifters"] every day.
We make decisions every day.
We have choices when we make these decisions.
Does this choice lead to greater sanity, or does it further the insanity?
We all make these choices.
We all are head monks in our own life, and we support the Shuso, and the Shuso knows and feels it, and we support each other, and I hope we all know and feel that too.
In this way, we all hold the world together.
I would like to do a little detour.
Practice period often means a period of increased practice.
That's so for me too.
I would like to say a word about breathing, and I don't know if there are any relative newcomers here.
We all know how to breathe.
Otherwise, we would not be sitting here, right?
Our bodies know how to breathe.
Fortunately, we are born with that knowledge.
The wisdom of our body knows how to breathe.
I would like to ask you to explore belly breathing.
Can I see a quick show of hands: who is usually belly breathing?
Belly breathing is what they usually tell you not to do.
It means not to fill up your lungs but to really breathe into your belly, into your gut, even though that's not what you breathe into.
You breathe always into your lungs.
But can you put your hands on your belly and do a big belly-breathing inhale?
When you exhale, don't do this, pressing your chest together, but just pull in your belly.
For the next inhale, don't do anything active, but just relax your belly.
Did you feel the difference, how effortless that inhale is?
I was lucky.
I had a karate teacher who really went after us when we didn't do belly breathing.
Those karate shouts, those kiai's you hear, they don't come from here.
They come from the real center of your whole body.
It comes from your gut.
It comes from your whole person.
If you've ever been the focus of a kiai, a spirit yell, spirit shout, well, you feel it.
It's like a physical impact.
It's quite amazing.
He told us to go on runs and only do belly breathing.
It's quite a difference, how this breath can inform us.
It becomes less of this shallow thing up here.
Especially in times of stress, it's amazing what this belly breath does, versus this.
If you have ever been in a physical fight, you don't want to do the shallow panting, though your body does it to get more air.
Bodies are very smart, but in truth that will carry you only through a few seconds of physical altercation.
Then you need to go to your whole-body breathing.
You need that belly breath.
So that was a brief detour into the gut of our zazen.
People are really awesome.
Yeah, we get stuck on different politics and different opinions and wanting people to be different, but people are just really awesome.
Last week, I found this little story, of all places, on Facebook.
It was a video: "Couple falls in love with wingless bumblebee."
A woman, her name was Shay, was out on a walk, and this little bumblebee bumbled into her path.
It had no wings.
She said she didn't know what moved her, but she bent down and offered that bumblebee her hand, and was really surprised when the little thing climbed up on her hand.
She took it home.
It was cute.
You saw in the video that she picked some lavender, put it in her palm, and the bumblebee was eating while they were walking home.
The woman realized that without wings, a bumblebee might not make it.
It wanted maybe some help, because it walked in her path and it walked onto her hand.
So she and her significant other started caring for this bumblebee.
They gave it little sponges filled with sugar water and honey, diluted honey.
They took it out for walks.
They took it out and put it on flowers.
She said that was so the bumblebee would not forget its native language and would get to interact with other winged creatures.

Two of my favorite quotes from that little video were "I thought I would take care of her, but I never thought I would love her," and the other one, "I thought I was taking care of her, but after a couple of weeks I felt she took care of me."
Bumblebees have short lives, but this little insect was a perfect Dharma teacher.
In its 30 days it taught its human students quite a bit.
They will never be the same again.
Mary Oliver, one of my favorite poets, wrote a poem, well, not quite about bumblebees, but about bees.
She called the poem "Hum."
"Hum" by Mary Oliver.
*What is this dark hum among the roses?
The bees have gone simple, sipping, that's all.
What did you expect, sophistication?
They're small creatures and they're filling their bodies with sweetness.
How could they not moan in happiness?
The little worker bee lives, I have read, about three weeks.
Is that long?
Long enough, I suppose, to understand that life is a blessing.
I have found them, haven't you?

Stopped in the very cups of the flowers, their wings a little tattered, so much flying about to the hive, then out into the world, then back, and perhaps dancing should the task be to be a scout, sweet, dancing bee.
I think there isn't anything in this world I don't admire.
If there is, I don't know what it is.
I haven't met it yet, nor expect to.*
*The bee is small, and since I wear glasses, so I can see the traffic and read books, I have to take them off and bend close to study and understand what is happening.
It's not hard.
It's, in fact, as instructive as anything I've ever studied.

Plus, too, it's love, almost too fierce to endure, the bee nuzzling like that into the blouse of the rose, and the fragrance and the honey and, of course, the sun, the pure sun shining all the while over all of us.*
I want to thank you for listening to my Dharma talk.
I appreciate that after this plentiful and fulfilling offering yesterday, you had the energy to come to today's event, too.
Now that we have entered the practice period, I encourage you to make extra effort to bring your practice into everyday life.
Lean into it a little bit more, and open up beyond what you usually do.
Open up to the world beyond what you think possible.
A world where a wingless bumblebee is loved and saved, and an Eno is graciously forgiven.
It's not such a bad place.
Maybe we need a breather.
Maybe we need some time for love and hope and compassion.
May you have peace.
May you practice with your difficulties and your choice.
And may you love.
I hope you got something out of today's Dharma talk.
And if not, could you do me a favor and utterly forget it and just continue your practice?
*May our intention equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.
Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to end them.
Buddha's way is unsurpassable.
I vow to become it.*
